children: By Paul Berger
The Logistics Report won't publish Monday, Sept. 7, the Labor Day holiday in the U.S. Look for us back in your inbox on Tuesday.
President Trump's tariff and electric-vehicle policies are colliding with Volkswagen's plans for the large and lucrative U.S. market.

The WSJ's Stephen Wilmot reports that Volkswagen is shaking up its U.S. leadership for the second time in two years as the world's second-largest carmaker aims to revive its American business. Veteran executive Marco Schubert will take over Volkswagen's business in North America in October.
The U.S.-with about 16 million total annual vehicle sales and a large potential for profit-has eluded Volkswagen for decades. The past 18 months have been particularly tough.

With just one small U.S. factory in Chattanooga, Tenn., Volkswagen imports most of the vehicles it sells in the U.S., making it one of the automakers worst affected by Trump's trade policies. The company estimates the annual hit to its business at the equivalent of $5.8 billion.
Tariffs have brought fresh urgency to the question of localizing production in America. In Chattanooga, Volkswagen only makes its Atlas and Atlas Cross Sport SUVs.

Volkswagen Chief Executive Oliver Blume has poured funds into Scout Motors to revive a historic sport-utility-vehicle brand as an all-American EV startup. A Scout factory under construction in South Carolina isn't set to deliver vehicles before 2028.
Volkswagen plans to slim down leadership teams and reduce its workforce by 50,000 positions, on top of roughly 50,000 already agreed to over the past two years. (WSJ)
Quote of the Day
Manufacturing

Ford Motor is setting an ambitious sales target for its new electric truck that has only been met by Tesla in the U.S. The WSJ's Ryan Felton writes that the automaker aims to sell more than 100,000 of the trucks in its first year of production. The truck, called the Ford Fathom, starts around $30,000 and will go on sale next year. Ford is seeking mainstream sales not seen by its earlier, more expensive electric vehicles.

The Fathom will be made on a built-from-scratch assembly line in Louisville, Ky. Executives have said the truck will feature technology designed to compete with Tesla and upstart Chinese automakers, with a price tag similar to mainstream sedans and SUVs. Ford will begin taking customer orders early next year. If it meets Ford's targets, Fathom would instantly become one of the top-selling EVs in the U.S. in the first year of its production.
Number of the Day
Average U.S. retail price for diesel on Thursday, according to the American Automobile Association, a four-year high and rising toward the record $5.816 a gallon set in 2022.

World food prices rose in August, with the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization food price index up 1.9% from July and was up 2.5% from a year earlier. (WSJ)
Victoria's Secret boosted its full-year outlook again. (WSJ)
Lululemon Athletica cut its outlook for the second time this year. (WSJ)
